passages.text: A Pilot Machine Learning Study Using Trauma Admission Data to Identify Risk for High Length of Stay
Introduction:

Trauma patients have diverse resource needs due to variable mechanisms and injury patterns. The aim of this study was to build a tool that uses only data available at time of admission to predict prolonged hospital length of stay (LOS).
Methods:

Data was collected from the trauma registry at an urban level one adult trauma center and included patients from 1/1/2014 to 3/31/2019. Trauma patients with one or fewer days LOS were excluded. Single layer and deep artificial neural networks were trained to identify patients in the top quartile of LOS and optimized on area under the receiver operator characteristic curve (AUROC). The predictive performance of the model was assessed on a separate test set using binary classification measures of accuracy, precision, and error.
Results:

2953 admitted trauma patients with more than one-day LOS were included in this study. They were 70% male, 60% white, and averaged 47 years-old (SD: 21). 28% were penetrating trauma. Median length of stay was 5 days (IQR 3–9). For prediction of prolonged LOS, the deep neural network achieved an AUROC of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.786–0.814) specificity was 0.95, sensitivity was 0.32, with an overall accuracy of 0.79.
Conclusion:

Machine learning can predict, with excellent specificity, trauma patients who will have prolonged length of stay with only physiologic and demographic data available at the time of admission. These patients may benefit from additional resources with respect to disposition planning at the time of admission.
Introduction

Achieving optimal outcomes in trauma with limited resources has been accomplished by improving trauma systems, understanding trauma epidemiology and streamlining patient flow and logistics. Resource allocation for trauma patients is difficult because injury severity, type-of-injury, and required resources are highly variable; the pattern of injury for two distinct patients experiencing the same mechanism (e.g., motor vehicle collision) may be vastly different from one another and therefore require a potentially broad set of resources. Understanding this variability is necessary to ensure an optimally functioning trauma system.

Many trauma systems group in-hospital patients by acuity (intensive care unit, step-down, floor, etc.), based on injury characteristics (e.g., non-operative trauma to an advanced practice service) or based on locations within the hospital where throughput or resources differ. These decisions often are made in the emergency department (ED) and are based on expectations of resource needs including anticipated hospital length of stay (LOS). Improved or automated methods of predicting which patients will have prolonged stays or higher resource needs during the first few hours of care may allow for creation and implementation of targeted interventions for this group of patients. Appropriate interventions could include clustering of high-risk patients into specialty care hospital units, developing focused pathways for the most complex patients, training care teams to manage these patients more effectively, or alerting discharge planning teams to engage such patients earlier in their hospital course. The same prediction tool would similarly enable us to set an expected LOS target and determine those that deviate from expectation in requiring either more or less resources than originally anticipated.

Due to electronic health record advances and integration, clinical prediction tools are increasingly common across medicine and surgery, changing the way clinicians predict and treat everything from venous thromboembolism prophylaxis to sepsis. Machine learning algorithms, sometimes referred to as artificial intelligence (AI), denote a collection of computational constructs that allow a computer program to “train” on data to make such predictions. This occurs over multiple executions of the program; each iteration is followed by an adaption in the program’s code based on results of the program’s previous predictions. These have been used throughout clinical medicine, and often provide greater accuracy and discrimination than conventional statistics because of these programs’ ability to “learn” as they see new data, making them more adaptive than many other modeling options. The utility of the deep learning paradigm in this situation is that it can segregate patients by complex multivariable interactions to capture the additive risks of each individual variable in a way that conventional statistics, or even sometimes humans, may not understand or be able to quantify. This is not designed to replace but enhance the current understanding of how multiple, seemingly unrelated variables may interact to effect clinical outcomes. Indeed, predicting LOS and understanding factors related to length of stay in trauma patients is not new. However, no study to our knowledge has attempted to predict length of stay of trauma patients with only the parameters available in the trauma bay or while the patient is still in the ED. A prediction tool that could identify patients at high risk for prolonged length of stay at this critical time point would be useful clinically and provide an opportunity for early identification and intervention and could provide a paradigm for building a tool to assess patients at different time points to help with resource allocation.

The goal of this project was to develop a prediction model to determine, at the time of admission, whether an injured patient will have a prolonged stay (in this study defined as >75th percentile LOS) using only clinical and diagnostic data available at the time of admission (before a patient leaves the ED), so that it may optimally guide triage, placement, and resource determinations.
Materials and Methods
Study Population and Data Source

Data were derived from the trauma registry at an urban level 1 trauma center. Data fields collected in this registry are governed by the Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems (MIEMSS). We included all adult trauma patients (age ≥18 years old) admitted to from January 1, 2014, to March 31, 2019. Patients discharged from the ED and those with LOS less than two midnights were excluded. Patients missing Injury Severity Score data or GCS data were also excluded.
Feature Selection and Model Initialization

The outcome of interest is high LOS. We chose to examine LOS as our primary outcome of interest and defined a threshold value at the 75th percentile as a proxy marker for patients requiring high resource utilization and who may benefit from earlier identification to allow for interventions aimed at LOS reduction. The 75th percentile for LOS was determined from the cohort and used as the cutoff for the binary classifier (i.e., we developed a model to predict if a patient would be under or over the 75th percentile). We chose to include presenting demographic and injury data in the analysis, while other information such as preexisting comorbidities or payor information may not be available or complete in the trauma bay and therefore were not included. This modeling paradigm potentially sacrifices predictability in exchange for increasing clinical utility of the tool at the time of admission. With this construction, the model may be useful for triaging patients to a more appropriate inpatient unit or allocating resources (such as ED social work, case management, or early multidisciplinary care attention) earlier in the hospital course to maximize their impact.

The selected features included were age in years, sex, Race, injury mechanism (blunt versus penetrating), GCS (eye, verbal, and motor) and ED disposition (floor, ICU, OR); with units and ranges as defined by the American College of Surgeons and MIEMSS. Abbreviated Injury Scores for each body region (AIS) 1–6, were included as a proxy admission-data based severity metric, as initial admission diagnoses are not readily available in the registry, and patients surviving past the two-midnight threshold have anecdotally few substantial updates and changes to the admission diagnoses in our patient population. We tabulate these data as well as measures of central tendency and spread for hospital length of stay for our included cohort.
Machine Learning Model

Artificial neural networks (ANN) were trained using offline MATLAB R2016b (version 9.1). We randomly partitioned patients into three groups for training and validation on the data set for each ANN: 85% were for training partition including 15% for cross-validation and 15% were reserved for testing of the ANN as a strategy to internally test the final model for performance metrics. The final ANN was not exposed to any of the final test patients (the 15% in the testing partition) until after the model finished training and validating. All patients by defined inclusion criteria had complete GCS and ISS data. Therefore, the final dataset had no missing data for any patient age, sex and ED disposition. Race was missing for 14 patients, and these were coded as such.

With this training paradigm established, we iteratively tested one, two, and three-hidden layer feed-forward neural networks with between 1 and 50 neurons per layer. Each of these models was trained using the scaled conjugate gradient back-propagation algorithm on the dedicated partition. This revealed the optimal architecture (area under the receiver operator characteristic curve (AUROC) was optimized) as a 3 hidden-layer, deep neural network with 35, 24 and 16 neurons, respectively, Figure 1. We tabulated confusion tables and statistics on the testing partition, as well as for the entire data set. We assessed the predictive ability of the model rigorously with various numerical measures of accuracy, precision, and error. 95% confidence intervals were generated by computing performance metrics over 100 unique, random data partitions.

A sensitivity analysis was performed to evaluate for an association between coded Race and performance characteristics within the model. Binary classification (under/over the 75th percentile) was compared against true LOS under/over 75th percentile classification for each race and these are compared using chi-squared statistics. The 14 patients with uncoded race were not included in this sensitivity analysis.
This study was approved by the Johns Hopkins Hospital Institutional review board and conducted with a waiver of consent as this is retrospectively analyzed data.
Results

2953 admitted trauma patients with length of stay greater than one-day length of stay (at least two midnights) were identified, Figure 2. Patients were predominantly male (70%), white (60%), and averaged 47 years-old (SD = 21). 28% of admitted patients were penetrating trauma patients (Table 1). Injury characteristics including AIS (Abbreviated Injury Severity Score) and GCS (Glasgow Come Scale) scores were also calculated, Figure 3. The median length of stay of included patients was 5 days (IQR 3–9). Patients in the 75th percentile of length of stay (>9 days) accounted for nearly half of total inpatient days among our cohort. Measures of spread and central tendency for length of stay were computed and shown graphically as a box plot, see Figure 3. Here length of stay is a non-normal, centrally clustered, right skewed beta distribution with outliers observed only on the right tail (range: 1–178).

The final multi-layer deep neural network model included three hidden layers with 35, 24, and 16 hidden neurons, respectively, Figure 1. This model was optimized during training and the final AUROC for the portion of the dataset reserved for testing (not previously seen by the model) was 0.80. When computed iteratively over 100 random data partitions, these AUC had SD 0.07 corresponding to a 95% CI of (0.786–0.814), Figure 4.

A confusion matrix and performance statistics were computed for the entire dataset, Table 2. This model was found to be highly specific, with specificity of 0.95. The model sensitivity was 0.32, with an overall accuracy of 0.79 on this dataset. Mathew’s correlation coefficient was 0.36.

Due to concerns about systematizing racial disparities, a post-hoc sensitivity analysis was performed examining differences in model performance across race. Patients were sub-grouped by race and final model performance recomputed. There was no difference in any performance metric between races or amongst those with unknown or missing race (P > 0.05 for all).
Discussion

Trauma patients have high variability in their injury patterns, the severity of their physiologic insult, in the clinical resources that they require, and in the time sensitivity of their conditions. In addition to the surgical and medical interventions required up front, many need case management, social work, early specialty care, and in-hospital disposition resources. We have developed a tool using clinical and demographic data available at the time of admission that predicts with good accuracy those patients which will have a prolonged length of stay (>75th percentile).

This algorithm remained robust without socioeconomic or insurance data that may not be readily available in real time. The model achieved an AUROC of 0.8, an overall accuracy of 79% and a specificity of over 95%. While the sensitivity was low (32%), these are overall compelling pilot results that point to the potential use of an ANN model to identify some high utilizers with high specificity, a premise that would allow us to identify and appropriately triage resources to these patients with the hopes of reducing their length of stay. Furthermore, while this was the chosen model, parameters for this cutoff are not fixed and performance of the model could be adjusted, e.g., by lowering the specificity requirement to increase sensitivity if a model with these parameters was desired. While previous data has suggested that many high LOS patients have non-physiologic reasons for delayed disposition, reasonable predictions of high LOS utilizers derived with only physiological trauma bay and early admission data suggest that this is also an important factor. Higher predictive ability could probably be obtained by including additional data, but the prediction might not be able to be made as early. Future models may combine the physiologic features here with additional patient-linked data to provide a more comprehensive model, or one that evolves throughout a patient’s stay to provide refined predictions at critical points of care (e.g., transfer out of the ICU) throughout the patient’s hospitalization. Such features may be key components of innovative changes in patient flow and care team organization in future care optimizing and resource saving institutional efforts.

This study provides a proof-of-concept modeling tool that could help optimize bed management and care planning for injured patients. In the most direct implementation, the model could, for example, obtain these data from the EMR and output anticipated LOS estimates with recommended destination nursing units and pre-populated consulting team orders to the ordering provider while admission orders are being placed or bed management when the room is being assigned. Levin et al. used a similar goal directed approach at model development to create a machine-learning model for discharge predictions that, when used at multidisciplinary rounds, decreased hospital length of stay. These are examples of clinical prediction tools designed with the end-user and end-timing in mind, which in turn maximizes the clinical applicability. A common pitfall in designing and implementing machine learning database projects is that the end result lacks clinical utility. For example, when the need for a prediction tool arises, but the developed tool interferes with clinical workflow, or there is substantial bias in the data source. This project began with an impact analysis of when a tool such as this would be needed (while admitting the patient), then predictive features for the model were selected from data that would likely be available at the point of utilization (i.e., clinical variables available at admission from the Emergency Department). We then chose a source that captures these data (or representatives thereof) at the time of admission with reasonable fidelity (the institutional trauma registry which captures data on all trauma service patient encounters admitted to the hospital). Using this inductive approach we developed a model, designed for user experience and ease of implementation, that prioritizes clinical utility.

At the current development stage, the algorithm is able, using only clinical and injury data available in the trauma bay, to predict which patients will be in the top quartile of LOS with good accuracy. Because no data was included from later in the hospitalization to make these predictions, this implies that the injury patterns, early hospital clinical characteristics and medical decision making (e.g., intubation) from the trauma bay are associated with high LOS. While this may be obvious to the experienced trauma surgeon, identifying the part of the care cycle providers to intervene upon to decrease LOS is important. This means that while there are probably other features from later in the hospitalization (e.g., development of pressure ulcers) that may also be associated with high LOS, much of the reason for high LOS is from early in the hospitalization. This finding means that decreasing LOS in these patients will be reliant on targeting pre-hospital and emergency department decision making, and that we can identify many of them as soon as they are admitted, possibly directing additional resources (e.g., social work, care planning, NP or PA attention) early in the hospitalization with the knowledge that they may be difficult to disposition and to identify what might resources can be delivered earlier than they otherwise would have been.

Predicting patient population segments with high resource utilization was the initial goal of this project. High resource utilization, however, has numerous definitions. This project aimed to identify trauma patients that would be high utilizers. Ultimately, we decided to start with high LOS as a surrogate for high utilization, recognizing that there are other definitions. High LOS was chosen because it is a direct representation of cost, and we have excellent data for this outcome, with very little missing data and high fidelity from both the trauma registry and administrative databases. This is something that other trauma centers will also have high quality data for, making these easily extrapolatable to their centers because of the ACS credentialing requirements. Eventually we hope to develop a collection of algorithms to predict not only high LOS, but also costs, need for surgery, ICU days, and other metrics which would be helpful for the providers to know and may also be intervenable.

Despite the promise of this pilot project, there are limitations. While specificity and predictive value are high in this patient population and geography, performance of this study at a single level 1 urban center study with a high percentage of penetrating trauma that may make these results less generalizable to other centers, though this limitation may be improved with the inclusion of more patients and broadening the model to include institutional factors. Our choice to use final-coded AIS scores as present (by design) in the trauma registry database as proxy indicators for admission diagnostic data introduces a degree of retrospective bias into the network, potentially exaggerating the precision of the predictive values reported. We felt this was the most appropriate and expedient source of data for this proof of concept study in this population, however, as our selection criteria for patients with an at least two-midnight stay limits the study to a sub-population in which confirmed diagnostic changes to the admission information (e.g. injuries found on autopsy, over-reads from initial radiological findings) are relatively uncommon and when occur typically only result in small changes in overall injury severity. More precise (re-) training and optimization of the algorithm may be done in concert with early implementation and validation, reducing the impact of any discrepancies in anticipated admission data, and would be best created in a prospective setting after this pilot endeavor. We also have not compared this model to an attending physician’s judgment at predicting high LOS patients, though, our model does provide a potential mechanism to automate and streamline the admission and bed management workflows, freeing up valuable cognitive and process-intensive resources including the surgeon’s ability to manage complex or multiple patients. Also, while appropriate for demonstration of the concept and designed with an implementation focus, this model is not yet incorporated within the electronic medical record (EMR).

Overall, we have developed a viable proof-of-concept model by which any user can predict, with excellent specificity, high utilizers within the admitted trauma population based on the metric of length of stay (>75 percentile). This may provide a signal early in the course of inpatient care for determining which patients will require additional resources with respect to care optimization, coordination, and disposition planning. Additional study in larger data sets could lead to development of more robust, generalizable models utilizing data that are available both at admission and throughout the hospital course. Further development of this pilot tool may allow for improvements in patient flow, bed management, and costs of care.
Conclusion

Artificial intelligence can predict which traumatically injured patients admitted to the hospital will be admitted for the longest period of time using only clinical and injury data that is available at the time of admission. This may be used to direct resources for optimal clinical care – targeting patients expected to have a prolonged length of hospital stay.

Schematic of the multilayer artificial neural network (ANN) constructed. 14 input variables were included, converging on 35 hidden nodes (first layer), then onto 24 hidden nodes (second layer), then onto 16 (third layer) hidden nodes (for simplicity, fewer nodes are shown). Each input variable connects, analogous to projections between neurons, to each hidden node within the next layer. Random “weights” are then applied to each neural connection. These weights are then modified dependent upon the data it is trained on, ultimately converging on the output layer, which is a binary prediction of high or low length of stay. Included Inputs were: age in years, sex, Race, injury mechanism (blunt versus penetrating), Abbreviated Injury Score 1–6, GCS (eye, verbal and motor) and ED disposition (floor, ICU, OR).
